h2: Radiography myths: what a radiograph can and cannot prove
html:
Radiography myths: what a radiograph can and cannot prove

A radiograph looks like proof, which is why its limits get forgotten. The myths below matter whether you shoot radiography yourself, buy it from a contractor or review the films. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the USA. Where a code requires it, the work goes to a licensed radiography contractor the owner hires, and we offer ultrasonic testing where the code and owner allow it, plus ASNT Level III review of the radiographs. The cross-method list is in conventional NDT myths.

Myth: If the IQI shows, the radiograph is acceptable

The image quality indicator is one of several checks a film must pass before anyone interprets it. Under ASME Section V Article 2, density in the area of interest must sit within limits (a 1.8 minimum for X-ray film, 2.0 for gamma, and 4.0 maximum for single-film viewing) and within minus 15 to plus 30 percent of the density through the essential hole or wire. A light "B" image on a darker background means backscatter protection was inadequate, and the film is rejected. Location markers must show that the whole area was covered. Check all of these before reading for flaws.

Myth: A radiograph shows how deep a flaw is

A radiograph is a shadow of the whole thickness projected onto one plane. It shows a flaw's length and its position along the weld, but not where it sits through the wall or how tall it is. Parallax shots from two source positions can estimate depth roughly, but crack height cannot be measured from a single radiograph. When an engineering assessment needs flaw height, the owner's engineer asks for ultrasonic sizing such as TOFD or tip diffraction, and that is where ultrasonic testing takes over.

Myth: Any RT Level II can run a gamma source in the USA

SNT-TC-1A certification covers the radiographic technique. Handling a gamma source is a licensed activity with its own rules. Under NRC regulations in 10 CFR Part 34, or the matching rules of an Agreement State, a radiographer must complete radiation safety training and at least two months of on-the-job training and be certified through a radiographer certification program run by a certifying entity. At a temporary job site, radiography may not be performed with only one qualified person present. X-ray machines fall under state radiation-control rules rather than Part 34. The technician needs both credentials, and the employer must hold the license.

Myth: The contractor's interpretation is the final word

The owner is entitled to check what it paid for, and an independent review can catch problems before they become repairs or rework. A Level III review starts with technique: IQI type and placement, density, backscatter, coverage and geometric unsharpness. Then it moves to interpretation against the acceptance code that applies, which is not always the one the contractor assumed. Disagreements are settled on the film, not on the report. For US projects, Atlantis's ASNT NDT Level III reviews radiographs and RT procedures produced by your licensed contractor; see outsourced Level III consulting.

Myth: A film interpreter is ready for digital images

Computed and digital radiography rest on the same physics but are read on a monitor, with adjustable contrast and brightness, measurement tools and their own image-quality checks. An interpreter who has read only film needs training and a practical examination on digital images, and the written practice should state which techniques each person is certified for. Radiographic testing training and the radiography simulator cover technique choice, IQI placement and image review without a source, and gamma radiography safety is taught as theory, not handled.
